paragraphs: Event sequences can differ in how events trigger later events, even when their timing is irregular. This paper groups sequences by modeling those underlying dynamics. Its mixture model assigns different clusters different Hawkes process parameters, so membership reflects a shared pattern of event generation rather than just a superficial resemblance between sequences.

The model uses a Dirichlet process prior over clusters and learns its parameters through variational Bayesian inference. The authors prove identifiability, providing a theoretical basis for distinguishing the mixture's components. They also introduce an adaptive strategy for allocating inner iterations, intended to accelerate convergence, and analyze both the data requirements and computational demands of learning.

Experiments on synthetic and real data indicate that the method can robustly uncover triggering structure in asynchronous sequences. It also achieves better clustering purity and consistency than the compared methods. These findings support the value of grouping sequences through a model of their generating processes, with theoretical analysis accompanying the practical learning procedure.
neurips-2017-a-dirichlet-mixture-model-o.tldr: A Dirichlet mixture of Hawkes processes clusters event sequences by their underlying triggering patterns.

paragraphs: Prediction systems often have to respect limits on computation, communication, response time, or the cost of obtaining features. This paper addresses those limits by allowing different inputs to consume different amounts of resources. The central idea is to use an inexpensive predictor where it is sufficiently accurate and reserve a more expensive model for harder cases.

The system learns both a low-cost prediction model and a gate that decides which model should handle each input. Training jointly optimizes prediction loss while imposing cost constraints. This connects routing decisions to the capabilities of the inexpensive model: the gate learns where that model can adequately approximate the expensive one.

Across several benchmark datasets, the approach achieves higher accuracy at the same cost than the compared state-of-the-art methods. The result supports adapting computation to the input instead of assigning every prediction the same budget. Its contribution is a joint learning formulation for deciding both how to predict cheaply and when the additional expense of a stronger model is justified.
neurips-2017-adaptive-classification-for.tldr: A jointly trained gate and inexpensive predictor reserve costly predictions for difficult inputs, improving benchmark accuracy at a fixed cost.

paragraphs: Hierarchical clustering builds a nested organization of data, but widespread use does not by itself explain what makes a hierarchy good. This paper develops theoretical guarantees using an objective that is dual to a framework introduced by Dasgupta. The objective supplies a common mathematical standard for examining several familiar clustering strategies.

For average linkage, which builds a hierarchy by merging groups, the authors prove a small constant approximation ratio. This bounds its performance relative to the best hierarchy under the chosen objective. For bisecting k-means, which repeatedly splits groups, they establish a poor lower bound on the approximation ratio, revealing potentially unfavorable behavior under that same standard.

The distinction does not imply that splitting-based approaches are inherently unsuccessful. The paper also provides two divisive algorithms with constant approximation guarantees. Together, these results show why the objective matters when judging a hierarchy: they give specific support for average linkage, identify a weakness of bisecting k-means, and demonstrate that other splitting strategies can retain strong guarantees.
neurips-2017-approximation-bounds-for-hi.tldr: A hierarchical clustering objective yields constant approximation guarantees for average linkage and two divisive algorithms, while exposing weak worst-case behavior for bisecting k-means.

paragraphs: Predicting gene expression from chromatin measurements requires handling many signals whose positions and interactions matter. The paper also treats interpretation as a central goal: a useful model should help identify relevant chromatin marks and how they work together. AttentiveChrome addresses prediction and interpretation within one architecture.

The model uses a hierarchy of Long Short-Term Memory modules to encode the spatially structured inputs and represent relationships among chromatin marks. Two jointly trained attention levels emphasize relevant marks and important positions within each mark. This gives the prediction system a way to weight both which signal matters and where its useful information occurs.

Evaluation across 56 human cell types finds improved predictive accuracy and better interpretation through attention scores than the compared feature visualization methods, including saliency maps. The finding supports integrating an explanatory weighting mechanism into the predictive model itself. The attention scores provide an interpretation of the model's decisions and the dependencies it learns, connecting its predictions to particular marks and locations.
neurips-2017-attend-and-predict-understa.tldr: AttentiveChrome jointly learns gene-expression predictions and attention over chromatin marks and positions, improving accuracy and interpretation across 56 cell types.

paragraphs: Euclidean k-means is computationally hard in the worst case, yet practical heuristics often work well. This paper investigates whether a property of the data can help explain that gap and support stronger algorithms. It studies additive perturbation stability: the optimal clustering is unique and remains unchanged when each point moves a little in Euclidean distance.

That condition formalizes tolerance to small measurement errors or uncertainty in point locations. For instances satisfying it, the authors design efficient algorithms that provably recover the optimal clustering. With an additional separation condition, they also obtain a simple, efficient algorithm that has theoretical guarantees and tolerates outliers.

The paper complements its theory by examining stability in real datasets and reporting good algorithmic performance on benchmark data. Its guarantees are tied to the stated stability and separation properties. The contribution is therefore a connection between a concrete form of data robustness and exact recovery, alongside evidence that studying this property can be relevant to practical clustering.
neurips-2017-clustering-stable-instances.tldr: Small-perturbation stability enables efficient, provably optimal k-means clustering, with outlier robustness under an additional separation condition.

paragraphs: This paper studies recovering a clustering by asking whether pairs of elements belong together. Each answer can be wrong with probability p, so collecting more judgments has to compensate for unreliable information. The aim is to identify the true groups while asking as few questions as possible, either interactively or with all questions chosen in advance.

The authors establish information-theoretic lower bounds on the required number of queries in both settings. They then design algorithms whose query requirements closely approach those bounds, including when the number of clusters is unknown. They also provide computationally efficient algorithms for adaptive and non-adaptive querying.

The framework is motivated by crowdsourced entity resolution, where people judge whether database records describe the same entity and each judgment has a cost. It also connects to predicting positive and negative social relationships, correlation clustering, and recovering groups from incomplete stochastic block model information. The results clarify how much noisy pairwise evidence clustering requires and provide constructive methods for using that evidence.
neurips-2017-clustering-with-noisy-queri.tldr: The paper bounds the noisy pairwise queries needed for clustering and develops algorithms that closely approach those bounds.

paragraphs: Large neural networks can require substantial memory and computation. Compression methods exploit their excess parameters, but many begin with a network trained without considering its later compression. This paper changes the training objective so that producing a compact model becomes part of learning from the outset.

The proposed regularizer encourages each layer's parameter matrix to have low rank. In plain terms, it favors matrices whose parameters can be represented through fewer independent directions. This links the structure learned during training to the structure that makes compression possible, rather than leaving all responsibility for compactness to a later processing step.

The authors report models that are substantially more compact while remaining at least as effective as those produced by the compared state-of-the-art compression techniques. The stated result supports treating training and compression as connected design decisions. Its significance is that an explicit preference for compressible parameter structure can improve the eventual size–effectiveness tradeoff, rather than requiring compactness to be pursued only after ordinary training has finished.
neurips-2017-compression-aware-training-.tldr: Encouraging low-rank layer parameters during training produces more compact models while preserving effectiveness in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: A measure designed to summarize average association can miss a relationship that is hidden or only potentially apparent. This paper treats discovering such potential correlations as a distinct measurement problem. It begins by proposing a set of natural properties that a suitable measure should satisfy, making the intended behavior explicit before choosing an estimator.

The authors show that the hypercontractivity coefficient, described through the rate of information bottleneck, satisfies all their proposed axioms. They then develop a method for estimating that coefficient from samples. This connects a theoretical characterization of potential correlation to a procedure that can be applied to observed data.

Numerical experiments find potential correlations among World Health Organization indicators and show robustness in discovering gene interactions from expression time series. In binary hypothesis tests on canonical potential-correlation examples, the estimator has greater statistical power than estimators of other correlation measures. These results support the proposed measure and estimator for the studied forms of hidden association, with the axioms specifying what the method is designed to capture.
neurips-2017-discovering-potential-corre.tldr: An estimator of the hypercontractivity coefficient detects potential correlations that average-association measures can miss.

paragraphs: Latent recommendation models are attractive for their accuracy and scalability, but much of their development has concentrated on user–item interactions. Cold start creates a different challenge: recommendations must remain useful when the interaction information normally supporting them is unavailable. DropoutNet introduces a neural latent model explicitly trained to handle that situation.

The main change concerns optimization. The authors use dropout to train neural networks for cold start, rather than adding separate content-based terms to the objective. This makes preparation for missing interaction information part of the training process. The proposed model can be placed on top of an existing latent model, extending it with cold-start capabilities and a deep architecture.

On publicly available benchmarks, the authors report state-of-the-art accuracy. The finding supports a training-centered approach to cold start and gives existing latent recommenders a route to handling it. The broader contribution is the observation that dropout can serve a task-specific purpose here: training the recommendation model to cope with the information conditions it will encounter during cold start.
neurips-2017-dropoutnet-addressing-cold-.tldr: DropoutNet uses dropout to explicitly train latent recommenders for cold start and reports state-of-the-art benchmark accuracy.

paragraphs: Sequence classifiers need a way to compare sequences. One approach counts matching pieces of length k, called k-mers. Allowing two pieces to match when their distance is at most m can improve classification, but it also makes similarity computation much more expensive. Existing algorithms therefore restrict the usable values of these parameters.

This paper develops techniques for accurately approximating pairwise similarity without paying the full computational cost. The approach allows much larger values of k and m, supporting higher predictive accuracy. The authors also solve an open combinatorial problem that had obstructed the scalability of earlier methods and provide theoretical bounds on approximation quality and running time.

Experiments evaluate the method on real biological and music sequence datasets. The results accompany the theoretical guarantees with evidence about practical approximation performance. More broadly, making these richer similarity measures affordable opens possibilities for sequence classification in audio, images, and text. Those wider applications are presented as opportunities enabled by the method, while the reported empirical evaluation concerns biological and music data.
neurips-2017-efficient-approximation-alg.tldr: Efficient similarity approximations make longer, more tolerant k-mer comparisons practical for sequence classification, with quality and runtime guarantees.

paragraphs: This paper considers optimization when decisions provide bandit feedback, meaning the learner receives limited information through its actions. The objective is a global loss depending on all the actions and need not be a sum of individual losses. That distinction expands the framework beyond problems whose success is measured solely by accumulated step-by-step loss.

The authors analyze Upper-Confidence Frank-Wolfe, an algorithm combining ideas from bandit methods and convex optimization. Its motivation is to bring techniques for decision making with incomplete feedback together with techniques for optimizing a global function. The paper establishes performance guarantees across different classes of objective functions and discusses whether those guarantees are optimal.

The contribution is a theoretical treatment of a broad optimization setting, with potential applications in statistics, machine learning, and other fields. Evaluating a global loss makes the collective effect of the actions central to the problem. The guarantees explain the algorithm's behavior for the function classes considered, while the optimality discussion addresses how close those results are to what can be achieved.
neurips-2017-fast-rates-for-bandit-optim.tldr: Upper-Confidence Frank-Wolfe receives theoretical guarantees for bandit optimization of global losses across several function classes.

paragraphs: Outlier detection usually begins after data have been collected, but obtaining those data can itself be expensive. This paper asks how to identify unusual objects while observations are still arriving. It models each object as an arm in a multi-armed bandit, turning the choice of what to measure next into part of the detection problem.

The authors formalize outlier-arm identification and propose two sampling strategies with theoretical guarantees. They analyze sampling efficiency, connecting the reliability of the eventual detection to the amount of information collected. The key change is that observation decisions and outlier detection are considered together instead of treating data acquisition as a completed preliminary step.

Experiments on synthetic and real data report a 70–99% reduction in data collection cost relative to the baseline, with nearly perfect accuracy. These are empirical findings for the evaluated settings. They show that deciding which objects to sample during detection can substantially reduce measurement costs while retaining strong accuracy, making the approach relevant when collecting observations is a major expense.
neurips-2017-identifying-outlier-arms-in.tldr: Two bandit sampling strategies identify outliers during data collection, reporting 70–99% cost savings with nearly perfect accuracy in experiments.

paragraphs: Designing heuristics for hard combinatorial problems often takes specialized knowledge and considerable experimentation. This paper explores learning such heuristics when the same type of optimization problem occurs repeatedly with different input data. Repeated structure gives a learning system an opportunity to discover useful decision rules across problem instances.

The proposed framework combines reinforcement learning with graph embeddings. A learned greedy policy builds a solution incrementally, choosing each action using a graph embedding network that represents the current state of the partial solution. The resulting policy serves as a general procedure for constructing solutions, while the representation supplies information about the particular graph and the progress already made.

The authors demonstrate effective learned algorithms for Minimum Vertex Cover, Maximum Cut, and Traveling Salesman problems. These examples show that the framework applies across several graph optimization tasks. The stated findings support automating part of heuristic design by learning from recurring problem structure, with effectiveness demonstrated for the evaluated problems rather than an asserted guarantee of optimal solutions for every instance.
neurips-2017-learning-combinatorial-opti.tldr: Reinforcement learning and graph embeddings learn greedy solution-building heuristics for several hard graph optimization problems.

paragraphs: Finding a best element and ordering an entire collection are related tasks, but noisy pairwise comparisons can make their information requirements very different. This paper studies both in a probably approximately correct setting, where the goal allows controlled uncertainty and approximation. It asks how comparison costs depend on the assumptions imposed on the comparison outcomes.

Under the single assumption of strong stochastic transitivity, maximum selection needs only a number of comparisons linear in the number of elements. Ranking, however, requires quadratically many. The result establishes a substantial gap between identifying a top choice and recovering an ordering under the same stated structural assumption.

The paper also studies the Borda-score metric without imposing assumptions on the comparisons. In that setting, maximum selection remains possible with linearly many comparisons, while ranking can be achieved with O(n log n) comparisons. These findings emphasize that complexity depends on both the comparison model and the meaning of a good answer. Changing to the Borda-score metric changes the ranking task and its attainable comparison cost.
neurips-2017-maxing-and-ranking-with-few.tldr: The comparison cost of selecting a maximum versus ranking depends sharply on the assumptions and scoring metric.

paragraphs: Factorization machines and polynomial networks represent polynomial prediction functions through efficient low-rank decompositions. This paper extends them to predict several outputs together, supporting settings such as multiple classes or multiple tasks. The central modeling decision is to let the different outputs share a common basis.

The authors express learning as the estimation of a three-way tensor whose slices use that shared basis, then give a convex formulation. They develop an efficient conditional gradient algorithm and prove global convergence despite a non-convex basis-selection step. This links a compact shared representation to an optimization method with a convergence guarantee.

On classification tasks, the algorithm combines strong accuracy with substantially sparser models than the compared existing methods. For recommendation, the authors combine it with a reduction from ordinal regression to multi-output classification and report better ranking accuracy than simple baselines. The findings support shared polynomial structure as a useful way to handle multiple outputs, with benefits demonstrated in both model sparsity and task performance.
neurips-2017-multi-output-polynomial-net.tldr: Shared-basis polynomial models support multiple outputs through a convex formulation and a globally convergent learning algorithm.

paragraphs: Online decisions sometimes face restrictions that are uncertain when an action is chosen. This paper extends online convex optimization to multiple stochastic functional constraints that are independently and identically generated at each round. The decision maker learns the realized constraints only after acting, so the method must manage uncertainty about feasibility as well as prediction or optimization loss.

The proposed algorithm has expected regret and constraint violations bounded by O(sqrt(T)), where T is the number of rounds. It also provides high-probability bounds of O(sqrt(T) log(T)) for both quantities. These sublinear bounds describe how cumulative performance shortfalls and violations grow over time; they do not require every individual decision to satisfy every realized constraint.

The formulation includes long-term constrained online optimization and both stochastic and deterministic constrained convex optimization as special cases. Experiments on real-world data center scheduling further support the algorithm's performance. The contribution is a unified treatment of decision quality and constraint control when restrictions become observable only after decisions have been made.
neurips-2017-online-convex-optimization-.tldr: An online optimization algorithm controls regret and constraint violations when i.i.d. stochastic constraints are revealed only after each decision.

paragraphs: PointNet processes point sets, but its design does not capture the local structure defined by distances between points. That limits its ability to recognize fine detail and handle complex scenes. PointNet++ addresses this by organizing point processing into a hierarchy that learns local patterns and then combines them at progressively broader scales.

The network repeatedly applies PointNet within nested partitions of the input set. Distances in the underlying metric space determine the local context used for learning. Because real point sets can have uneven sampling density, the paper also introduces layers that adaptively combine features from multiple scales, addressing the performance loss associated with training on uniformly sampled data.

Experiments show efficient and robust learning of deep point-set features, with significantly better results than the compared state-of-the-art methods on challenging 3D point-cloud benchmarks. The findings support two linked architectural choices: explicitly representing local geometry and combining information across scales. Together, they let the model capture fine patterns while also incorporating the wider context around them.
neurips-2017-pointnet-deep-hierarchical-.tldr: PointNet++ learns hierarchical local features and adaptively combines scales to handle point clouds with varying sampling density.

paragraphs: Weight initialization affects how signals and gradients travel through a deep network. Keeping the average squared singular value of the input–output Jacobian at order one helps avoid exponentially shrinking or growing gradients. This paper studies a stronger property, dynamical isometry, in which the singular values concentrate near one, preserving signal magnitudes across directions.

Using free probability theory, the authors calculate the full singular-value distribution and examine its dependence on depth, initialization, and activation function. Their analysis finds that ReLU networks cannot achieve dynamical isometry in the setting studied. Sigmoidal networks can achieve it, but orthogonal weight initialization is required.

Experiments show that deep nonlinear networks achieving dynamical isometry learn orders of magnitude faster than those that do not. Properly initialized deep sigmoidal networks also consistently outperform deep ReLU networks in the reported comparisons. The paper's design lesson is to consider the full distribution of signal amplification, beyond its average, when initializing deep networks. Its theoretical and empirical results connect that distribution to learning speed.
neurips-2017-resurrecting-the-sigmoid-in.tldr: The paper links dynamical isometry to faster learning and shows how orthogonal initialization enables it in deep sigmoidal networks.

paragraphs: Making individual network weights sparse does not automatically make computation faster, because the remaining weights may be scattered throughout the model. This paper targets structured sparsity instead: removing whole neurons or convolutional channels. Those removals align pruning with the network's computational organization.

The proposed Bayesian model injects noise into neuron outputs while leaving weights unregularized. It uses a proper truncated log-uniform prior and a truncated log-normal variational approximation. This choice allows the KL term in the evidence lower bound to be calculated in closed form, supporting the model's learning procedure. Elements with low signal-to-noise ratios are then removed from the computation graph.

The authors report significant acceleration across several deep neural architectures. They also describe the method as straightforward to implement through a separate layer resembling dropout. The contribution connects probabilistic noise modeling to practical structural removal: the learned noise provides a basis for identifying expendable elements, and pruning those elements changes the actual computation performed by the network.
neurips-2017-structured-bayesian-pruning.tldr: A Bayesian noise model prunes whole neurons or channels with low signal-to-noise ratios, producing structured sparsity and reported acceleration.

paragraphs: Selecting the best fixed-size subset becomes harder when evaluating a candidate gives an unreliable score. This paper studies noisy monotone objectives, allowing both additive and multiplicative noise. It does not require submodularity, the diminishing-returns property assumed in some earlier work, so its setting covers a broader class of subset-selection objectives.

The authors first analyze how noise affects approximation ratios for greedy selection and POSS, two methods used in noise-free settings. They then introduce PONSS by adding a noise-aware strategy to POSS. Its improved approximation guarantee depends on assumptions that include independently and identically distributed noise; the theoretical improvement is therefore conditional on the stated noise setting.

Experiments on influence maximization and sparse regression report superior performance for PONSS. These results complement the analysis by showing benefits in two application areas. The central contribution is to treat unreliable evaluations as part of algorithm design, rather than assuming that methods effective with exact scores retain the same behavior when those scores are disturbed.
neurips-2017-subset-selection-under-nois.tldr: PONSS adapts subset selection to noisy evaluations, improving approximation guarantees under stated noise assumptions and performance in two application settings.

paragraphs: Subspace clustering groups points according to which underlying subspace they occupy. Many methods first assign pairwise affinities and then cluster the resulting graph. This paper proposes a geometric way to construct those affinities, using tangent cones associated with the convex hull of normalized data points.

A tangent cone describes the local directions available from a point within this convex geometry. The paper argues that the collection of underlying subspaces creates a strong association between a sample's tangent cone and its original subspace. Its conic subspace clustering algorithm uses a tangent-cone membership test to estimate how strongly pairs of samples should be connected.

The authors provide deterministic and stochastic guarantees for the learned affinity matrix, including its true-positive and false-positive rates and spread. These properties translate directly into overall clustering accuracy. The contribution therefore connects a geometric view of the data to both a practical clustering procedure and an analysis of the relationships it constructs, making affinity estimation the bridge between subspace structure and final groups.
neurips-2017-subspace-clustering-via-tan.tldr: Conic subspace clustering uses tangent-cone geometry to estimate pairwise affinities, with guarantees connecting those affinities to clustering accuracy.

paragraphs: Understanding a neural network requires comparing the representations it learns across layers, networks, or stages of training. SVCCA provides a fast way to make those comparisons while remaining invariant to affine transformations. This allows representations to be compared even when their coordinate descriptions differ, making similarity less dependent on the particular form of their encoding.

The authors use the method to estimate the intrinsic dimensionality of layers and find unnecessary over-parameterization in some cases. They also track representation changes during training, observing that convergence toward final representations proceeds from lower layers upward. Another application examines where information specific to individual classes emerges within a network.

These analyses suggest training regimes that save computation and reduce overfitting. The paper's contribution combines a comparison tool with examples of what such comparisons can reveal about learning. Its speed permits more comparisons than previous methods, while its invariance makes comparisons across different layers and networks meaningful. The reported findings connect representation analysis to both interpretation and changes in training practice.
neurips-2017-svcca-singular-vector-canon.tldr: SVCCA efficiently compares neural representations, revealing excess dimensionality, bottom-up convergence, and opportunities to improve training.

paragraphs: Sequential decision problems require both finding good plans and generalizing what those plans teach. Expert Iteration separates these responsibilities between tree search and a deep neural network. Search develops improved policies, while the network learns to generalize the resulting plans into a policy that can guide later decisions.

The two components then improve one another. Once trained, the neural policy guides subsequent tree search, allowing search to produce stronger plans that supply further learning material. This creates an iterative relationship between explicit planning and learned generalization. The paper contrasts this division of labor with standard deep reinforcement learning approaches that rely on a network to both discover and generalize plans.

In Hex, Expert Iteration outperforms REINFORCE when training a neural network policy. The final tree-search agent, trained from scratch, also defeats MoHex1.0, identified in the abstract as the latest publicly released Olympiad champion. These results demonstrate the approach in a concrete planning task and support using search and neural learning as mutually improving components.
neurips-2017-thinking-fast-and-slow-with.tldr: Expert Iteration alternates tree-search planning with neural policy learning, producing strong Hex play through mutual improvement.

paragraphs: Probability models over structured objects must represent combinations such as complete routes, rankings, or graph matchings. Probabilistic Sentential Decision Diagrams, or PSDDs, provide a framework for learning distributions over such objects. This paper examines their scalability for routes on a map, asking how to retain manageable computation as the map becomes larger.

The authors introduce hierarchical route distributions and show how to use them to construct tractable PSDDs. The hierarchy gives route modeling an organization that supports scaling to larger maps. The contribution concerns both representing distributions over routes and learning them within a computationally manageable framework.

An empirical route-prediction task illustrates the model's usefulness, showing that prediction accuracy can increase significantly relative to Markov models. This result provides an application-level reason to pursue the hierarchical construction, beyond scalability alone. The paper connects a general framework for structured probability to a specific modeling domain, demonstrating how a hierarchy over routes can support tractable models with improved prediction in the reported evaluation.
neurips-2017-tractability-in-structured-.tldr: Hierarchical route distributions make PSDD route models tractable on larger maps and improve route prediction over Markov models in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: Unsupervised image translation learns relationships between image domains using separate image collections. The difficulty is that these collections reveal each domain's distribution but do not uniquely determine how images across domains should correspond. Infinitely many joint distributions can share the same individual distributions, so additional assumptions are needed.

The paper introduces a shared-latent-space assumption and builds a translation framework based on Coupled GANs. The assumption supplies a common underlying representation through which the domains can be related. This is central to the method: it gives structure to a correspondence problem that the separate image collections alone cannot resolve.

Comparisons with competing approaches show high-quality translations for street scenes, animals, and faces. The framework is also applied to domain adaptation, where it achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets. These findings demonstrate useful translations and adaptation under the proposed modeling approach. They support the shared representation as a productive assumption for the evaluated tasks, while preserving the paper's distinction between learning individual image distributions and specifying relationships between them.
neurips-2017-unsupervised-image-to-image.tldr: A shared-latent-space assumption enables a Coupled GAN framework to learn image translation from separate domain collections.
